title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the shortened pattern, the affirmative any and the evidence

questions.prompt: A reading club buys its second-hand books from the families of Bizerte. It wants one short line for the notice on its door, saying this and nothing more: of two books in the same state, the club will always take the one that costs less. English lets both halves of a parallel change lose the verb be together with its subject. Which line does the club print?

options.text: The cheapest, the best.
Cheaper, better.
The cheaper, the better.
The more cheap, the better.

questions.explanation: "The cheaper, the better." is the line: when the two halves of a parallel change would hold nothing but the verb be and its subject, English drops them both and leaves the two comparatives standing, each with its own the. "The cheapest, the best." replaces the two comparatives by superlatives; a superlative ranks one item above all the others, and the club is not hunting for the single cheapest book in the town, it is stating a rule that holds of any two books it is offered. "Cheaper, better." throws away both the, and those two small words are the whole of what holds the halves together; without them the line falls into two loose words. And "The more cheap, the better." marks the first comparative twice over: cheap is a short adjective, so it builds its comparative with -er and never with more.

questions.prompt: A book fair in Monastir is printing the notice that will stand at its entrance. The fair has twenty stalls, and the notice has to carry one idea and no other: it does not matter which stall a visitor walks up to, every single one of them will take an order for a book that is not on its shelves. Which sentence carries that meaning?

options.text: Some stall will take an order for a book it does not have.
Any stall will take an order for a book it does not have.
Any stall will not take an order for a book it does not have.
No stall will take an order for a book it does not have.

questions.explanation: "Any stall will take an order for a book it does not have." carries it exactly: inside an affirmative statement, any is not asking whether such a stall exists, it means practically every one, so take whichever stall you like and the sentence still holds. This is also the one use in which any stands in front of a singular noun, stall, instead of a plural or an uncountable one. "Some stall will take an order for a book it does not have." points at one particular stall the writer cannot name, which is the opposite of it does not matter which. "No stall will take an order for a book it does not have." tells the visitor that not one of the twenty will help. And "Any stall will not take an order for a book it does not have." pushes an any- word in front of a negative verb, a place English never gives it; when the whole sentence is negative the negative comes first, no stall will take an order.

questions.prompt: Read this short piece from a regional paper, then answer. "Ten years ago the Gafsa music fair sold tickets only at its own gate. This year it sold seven out of ten before the gates opened, most of them from a telephone. Its director says the fair now spends more on its website than on posters, and that the two evenings it added in 2024 were both full." The director claims that the fair no longer needs its posters as much as it once did. Which detail of the piece supports that claim most directly?

options.text: The fair now spends more on its website than on posters.
Seven tickets out of ten were sold before the gates opened.
The fair added two evenings in 2024 and both were full.
The fair sold tickets only at its own gate ten years ago.

questions.explanation: "The fair now spends more on its website than on posters." is the supporting detail, because it is the only line that weighs the posters against something else, and a claim about posters needs a fact in which posters appear. "Seven tickets out of ten were sold before the gates opened." proves that selling early works, and the piece adds that most of those sales came from a telephone, which points the same way; but no figure in that sentence weighs the posters against anything, so it supports the claim only at one remove. "The fair added two evenings in 2024 and both were full." shows that the fair is bigger than it was, which is a different claim altogether. And "The fair sold tickets only at its own gate ten years ago." describes the old arrangement; it sets the scene without measuring anything about today.

questions.prompt: The photography club of Nabeul hangs its prints in a room whose lamps can be turned down. Its members have noticed that the further they lower the light, the smaller the number of details a visitor is able to make out. Which single sentence states that rule?

options.text: The darker the room, the less details a visitor can make out.
The darkest the room, the fewest details a visitor can make out.
The more dark the room, the fewer details a visitor can make out.
The darker the room, the fewer details a visitor can make out.

questions.explanation: "The darker the room, the fewer details a visitor can make out." states the rule: parallel change ties two movements together and never demands that they go the same way, so the first half may rise while the second falls, as long as each half keeps its the and its comparative. "The darker the room, the less details a visitor can make out." chooses the wrong comparative of quantity: details are counted one by one, and a countable plural takes fewer, while less belongs to what cannot be counted, less light, less time. "The darkest the room, the fewest details a visitor can make out." replaces both comparatives by superlatives, which rank one item above the rest instead of linking two changes. And "The more dark the room, the fewer details a visitor can make out." builds the comparative of a short adjective with more, where dark takes -er.

questions.prompt: A journalist has written two sentences about the same market and has to choose one noun for each gap. Sentence 1: "Sales fell slowly and steadily over eight years: a long, quiet ___." Sentence 2: "In the week that followed the news, sales fell by half: a ___ nobody had expected." Which noun belongs in the second gap?

options.text: decline
casualty
plunge
shortage

questions.explanation: "plunge" belongs in the second gap: a plunge is a fall that is sudden and steep, and half the sales lost inside a single week is exactly that. "decline" is the noun the first gap wants, a fall that is slow and steady and spread over years, which is why the journalist wrote long and quiet in front of it. "casualty" names whoever suffers because of an event, and not the event itself: the small shops that closed were the casualties of the fall, while the fall was what struck them. And "shortage" is the situation of not having enough of something; a week in which half the buyers stopped buying is not a week in which the discs ran out, and the two must not be confused.

questions.prompt: Four lines from a magazine article use words of this theme. Three of them build the word into a construction English allows. In which line is the word built wrongly?

options.text: The old reading room is the lifeblood of the whole club.
The city magazine paid tribute for the woman who opened the first record shop.
A study blamed the price of the discs for two years of falling sales.
Half the village could not read, and the new evening class set out to fight that illiteracy.

questions.explanation: "The city magazine paid tribute for the woman who opened the first record shop." is built wrongly: to pay tribute is followed by to before the person being honoured, and that to belongs to the expression, so the line needs paid tribute to the woman who opened the first record shop. The three others are built as English builds them. "The old reading room is the lifeblood of the whole club." keeps of after lifeblood, which is a noun. "A study blamed the price of the discs for two years of falling sales." uses one of the two shapes blame allows, blaming a thing or a person for a result; the other shape turns the sentence round, blamed two years of falling sales on the price of the discs, and a line that puts on after blame and for further on has borrowed half of each and belongs to neither. And "Half the village could not read, and the new evening class set out to fight that illiteracy." uses the noun English forms from literacy by putting the negative prefix in front of it.
